images.caption: The fortified Monnow Bridge at Monmouth.

name: Chepstow
lead: The oldest stone castle in Britain, at the mouth of the Wye.
intro: Chepstow guards the mouth of the Wye where it meets the Severn, and its castle — begun in 1067 — is the oldest surviving stone fortification in Britain. It is the southern gateway to the valley, minutes from the old Severn Bridge and the closest Welsh town to Bristol.
staying: The most accessible Wye Valley base from England, with the castle, racecourse and town on hand and the gorge opening out to the north. Good for a short break with minimal driving.
thingsToDo: Chepstow Castle and the town walls; the racecourse; the start of the Wye Valley Walk and Offa's Dyke Path north to Tintern; and the tidal Severn views from the old bridge.
whenToVisit: Year-round; autumn for the valley, and race days bring crowds. Very close to Bristol and the M4/M48.
localTip: Start the riverside walk from Chepstow up to Tintern along the old railway and Offa's Dyke — it is the best way to arrive at the abbey, on foot through the gorge rather than by car.

faqs.q: Is Chepstow Castle the oldest in Britain?
faqs.a: Chepstow Castle is generally regarded as the oldest surviving stone-built castle in Britain, with construction beginning in 1067, soon after the Norman Conquest. It stands dramatically on cliffs above the River Wye and is open to visitors.

faqs.q: How close is Chepstow to Bristol?
faqs.a: Very close — Chepstow sits just over the Severn from England, roughly 30 to 40 minutes from Bristol via the M48 Severn Bridge. That makes it the most easily reached part of the Wye Valley for visitors coming from the West Country and the M4 corridor.

images.alt: Chepstow Castle standing on cliffs above the River Wye
images.caption: Chepstow Castle above the tidal River Wye.

name: Llandogo
lead: A riverside village climbing the wooded gorge.
intro: Llandogo is a small village on the Welsh bank of the Wye between Tintern and Monmouth, its cottages climbing steeply up the wooded valley side. Once a river port for Bristol trows, it is now a quiet walking base in the heart of the gorge.
staying: A peaceful riverside base right in the middle of the valley's best scenery, within a few minutes of Tintern and Monmouth both.
thingsToDo: The walk up to Cleddon Shoots waterfall behind the village; the riverside path along the Wye; Offa's Dyke on the ridge above; and easy reach of Tintern Abbey.
whenToVisit: Autumn for the woodland colour; spring for the waterfalls after rain. A quiet base year-round.
localTip: Follow the steep path up behind the village to Cleddon Shoots, a tall woodland waterfall that runs hardest after wet weather and is often completely deserted.

faqs.q: Is Llandogo a good quiet base in the Wye Valley?
faqs.a: Yes. Llandogo is a small, peaceful village midway between Tintern and Monmouth, set on the river amid the steep woods of the gorge. It offers riverside and hillside walks from the door and easy access to the valley's highlights without the traffic of the bigger towns.

faqs.q: What is Cleddon Shoots?
faqs.a: Cleddon Shoots is a woodland waterfall on the hillside above Llandogo, tumbling through the trees of the Wye gorge. It is reached by a steep footpath from the village and is at its most dramatic after rain.

name: Trellech
lead: Standing stones and a lost medieval town on the hill.
intro: Trellech sits on the hills above the Wye gorge and was, briefly in the 13th century, one of the largest towns in medieval Wales before it dwindled to a village. It keeps three prehistoric standing stones — "Harold's Stones" — that give it its name, and wide views over the surrounding country.
staying: An elevated, rural base above the valley with more space and bigger views than the riverside villages, and Monmouth and Tintern both a short drive away.
thingsToDo: Harold's Stones and the "Virtuous Well"; the large medieval church; the walks over the hills towards the Wye gorge; and the archaeology of the buried medieval town.
whenToVisit: Spring to autumn for the walks and views; a quiet base in any season.
localTip: Seek out the three leaning "Harold's Stones" in a field on the edge of the village — a Bronze Age alignment thousands of years older than the medieval town around it.

faqs.q: What are Harold's Stones at Trellech?
faqs.a: Harold's Stones are a row of three tall, leaning standing stones on the edge of Trellech, dating from the Bronze Age. They give the village its name (loosely "three stones") and are among the notable prehistoric monuments of the Wye Valley area.

faqs.q: Was Trellech ever a large town?
faqs.a: Yes — in the 13th century Trellech was one of the largest towns in medieval Wales, an industrial and market centre, before decline and plague reduced it to a village. Archaeological work in the surrounding fields has explored the remains of this "lost" town.

name: Conwy
lead: A complete ring of medieval walls around a castle town.
intro: Conwy is one of the great walled towns of Europe, its medieval ramparts still circling the town intact, anchored by Edward I's castle at the estuary mouth. Both are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the quay below holds what is claimed to be the smallest house in Britain.
staying: A superb, characterful base at the seaward end of the valley, with the castle, walls, quay and restaurants all within the walls, and Snowdonia rising immediately behind.
thingsToDo: Conwy Castle and the full circuit of the town walls; the Smallest House in Great Britain on the quay; Plas Mawr, a perfectly preserved Elizabethan townhouse; and mussels from the estuary.
whenToVisit: Year-round; the town is atmospheric even in winter. Summer and half-terms are busy on the main north Wales route.
localTip: Walk the full circuit of the town walls at opening time — the complete medieval circuit, with the castle, estuary and mountains all in view, is one of the best short walks in Wales and empty first thing.

faqs.q: Can you walk the town walls in Conwy?
faqs.a: Yes. Conwy has one of the most complete sets of medieval town walls in Britain, and much of the circuit is open to walk, giving elevated views over the castle, the estuary and the mountains behind. The walls and castle together form part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

faqs.q: Where is the smallest house in Britain?
faqs.a: The Smallest House in Great Britain stands on the quay at Conwy — a tiny red cottage just over three metres high and less than two metres wide, lived in until the early 20th century. It is open to visitors for a small charge.

images.alt: Conwy Castle and the walled town above the estuary
images.caption: Conwy Castle and the walled town.

name: Llanrwst
lead: An ancient bridge and a tea room that leans.
intro: Llanrwst is a market town in the middle of the Conwy valley, famous for the graceful stone bridge — attributed to Inigo Jones — that arches over the river to the tiny, crooked cottage of Tu Hwnt i'r Bont, now a tea room draped in Virginia creeper. Behind it rises the Gwydir Forest.
staying: A well-placed valley base between Conwy and Betws-y-Coed, with farmland and forest around it and the mountains close, usually at better value than either honeypot.
thingsToDo: The Pont Fawr bridge and Tu Hwnt i'r Bont tea room; the Gwydir Forest and its old lead-mine tracks and lakes; Gwydir Castle, a restored Tudor house; and the walks up either side of the valley.
whenToVisit: Autumn is when the creeper on Tu Hwnt i'r Bont turns red and the forest colours; spring and summer for the walking.
localTip: Head into the Gwydir Forest above the town for the old mine tracks and quiet lakes — it stays almost empty even when Betws-y-Coed just up the road is packed.

faqs.q: What is Tu Hwnt i'r Bont?
faqs.a: Tu Hwnt i'r Bont is a 15th-century stone cottage beside the Pont Fawr bridge in Llanrwst, now a National Trust tea room. It is famous for the Virginia creeper covering its walls, which turns vivid red in autumn and makes it one of the most photographed buildings in the Conwy valley.

faqs.q: Is Llanrwst a good base for the Conwy Valley?
faqs.a: Yes. Llanrwst sits centrally in the valley between Conwy and Betws-y-Coed, with the Gwydir Forest on its doorstep and the mountains close. It tends to be quieter and better value than the busier towns at each end of the valley.

name: Trefriw
lead: A Victorian spa village and a working woollen mill.
intro: Trefriw is a small village on the west side of the Conwy valley that grew as a Victorian spa around its chalybeate wells, and still runs a working woollen mill powered by the river. Above it the Gwydir Forest and a chain of hill lakes climb towards the mountains.
staying: A quiet, characterful valley base with the forest and lakes immediately behind and Betws-y-Coed and Conwy both a short drive away.
thingsToDo: The Trefriw Woollen Mill and the spa wells; the walk up to Llyn Crafnant and Llyn Geirionydd in the hills above; and the forest tracks of Gwydir.
whenToVisit: Spring to autumn for the lakes and forest walks; the mill is a year-round wet-weather option.
localTip: Walk or drive up to Llyn Crafnant above the village — a serene hill lake ringed by forest and crags that feels far more remote than the short climb to reach it.

faqs.q: What is Trefriw known for?
faqs.a: Trefriw is known for its working woollen mill, water-powered on the river, and for its Victorian spa heritage based on iron-rich chalybeate wells. Above the village, the hill lakes of Crafnant and Geirionydd and the Gwydir Forest offer excellent walking.

faqs.q: What walks are there near Trefriw?
faqs.a: The standout walks from Trefriw climb into the hills to Llyn Crafnant and Llyn Geirionydd, two scenic lakes ringed by forest and crag, with a circular route linking them. The wider Gwydir Forest offers many quieter tracks and old mine paths.

name: Llandudno
lead: The grand dame of Welsh seaside resorts.
intro: Llandudno is the largest and most elegant seaside resort in Wales, a sweeping Victorian promenade curving between two headlands beneath the great limestone hump of the Great Orme. It grew as a planned resort in the 1850s and has kept its pier, its tramway and its period grandeur.
staying: A polished seaside base just north of the Conwy valley, good for those who want a proper promenade, hotels and a pier alongside easy access to Snowdonia and Conwy.
thingsToDo: The pier and the promenade; the Great Orme by tramway, cable car or the toll road, with its summit views and wild goats; the Alice in Wonderland trail; and the beaches on either headland.
whenToVisit: Year-round as a resort; summer for the beach and pier. It is busy on fine weekends given its size and rail links.
localTip: Ride the Victorian tramway up the Great Orme rather than driving — it hauls you up the headland on cables laid in 1902, and the summit has the views, the goats and a Bronze Age copper mine.

faqs.q: What is there to do in Llandudno?
faqs.a: Llandudno offers a classic Victorian seaside experience — a long promenade, a pier, and the Great Orme headland reached by tramway or cable car, with summit views, wild Kashmiri goats and an ancient copper mine. There is also an Alice in Wonderland trail, linked to the town's connection with the real Alice Liddell.

faqs.q: Is Llandudno a good base for Snowdonia and Conwy?
faqs.a: Yes. Llandudno sits at the seaward end of the Conwy valley, with the walled town of Conwy a few minutes away and Snowdonia within about 30 to 40 minutes. It suits visitors who want a full-service seaside resort as a base for exploring the mountains and coast.

images.caption: Llandudno pier and bay from the Great Orme.

name: Llangollen
lead: The Dee, a steam railway and an aqueduct in the sky.
intro: Llangollen sits in a bend of the fast-flowing Dee in the south of the range, a compact town packed with attractions: a steam railway, a canal wharf, a ruined hilltop castle and, just downstream, Thomas Telford's astonishing Pontcysyllte Aqueduct. It hosts the International Musical Eisteddfod each July.
staying: The liveliest base in the Clwydian and Dee Valley area, with the most to do on the doorstep and easy reach of Snowdonia's eastern edge.
thingsToDo: The Llangollen Railway and the horse-drawn canal boats; the walk up to Castell Dinas Brân; the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct towpath; and the Horseshoe Falls and Horseshoe Pass drive.
whenToVisit: Spring to autumn for the outdoor attractions; July for the Eisteddfod, when the town is full. Autumn for the Dee valley colour.
localTip: Walk the towpath across the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct — 126 feet above the Dee with a drop straight off the water side and no railing — then reward yourself back in town. It is a World Heritage Site and unforgettable.

faqs.q: Can you walk across the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct?
faqs.a: Yes. A towpath runs alongside the canal channel across Pontcysyllte Aqueduct, 126 feet above the River Dee near Llangollen. There is a railing on the towpath side but only open water on the other, making it a spectacular — and for some, vertiginous — walk. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

faqs.q: What is there to do in Llangollen?
faqs.a: Llangollen packs in a heritage steam railway, horse-drawn canal boat trips, the hilltop ruin of Castell Dinas Brân, the Pontcysyllte Aqueduct and the scenic Horseshoe Pass, all within a few minutes. It also hosts the International Musical Eisteddfod each July.

images.caption: The Dee and the bridge at Llangollen.

name: Ruthin
lead: A medieval market town right under the ridge.
intro: Ruthin is a handsome medieval market town in the Vale of Clwyd, gathered on a low hill around a square of timber-framed and Georgian buildings, directly beneath the Clwydian ridge. Its old gaol and craft centre draw visitors, and the hills rise straight from the edge of town.
staying: The best-placed base for walking the Clwydian Range itself, with Moel Famau and the ridge hillforts on the doorstep and the vale's gentle countryside around.
thingsToDo: The walk up to Moel Famau and its Jubilee Tower; Ruthin Gaol and the Craft Centre; the medieval town square; and the Offa's Dyke Path along the ridge.
whenToVisit: Late summer and early autumn for the heather on the ridge; the town is a year-round, low-season base.
localTip: Climb Moel Famau from the Bwlch Penbarras car park above Ruthin for the shortest route to the ridge's highest point and its ruined Jubilee Tower, with both the vale and the coast in view.

faqs.q: Is Ruthin a good base for walking the Clwydian Range?
faqs.a: Yes — Ruthin sits directly beneath the Clwydian ridge in the Vale of Clwyd, making it the most convenient town for climbing Moel Famau, the range's highest point, and walking the Offa's Dyke Path along the hillfort-topped ridge.

faqs.q: What is Moel Famau?
faqs.a: Moel Famau is the highest hill in the Clwydian Range, topped by the ruined Jubilee Tower begun in 1810 to mark George III's jubilee. It is a popular, non-technical walk with wide views over the Vale of Clwyd, Snowdonia and, on clear days, the coast and beyond.

name: Mold
lead: A market town, a theatre and the eastern gateway.
intro: Mold is the county town of Flintshire at the eastern end of the range, closest to the motorway and the cities of the north-west. It is a lively market town with a strong cultural anchor in Theatr Clwyd, and the country park of Loggerheads and the ridge lie just to the west.
staying: The most accessible base in the Clwydian area from Manchester, Liverpool and Chester, good for those who want the ridge without a long drive to reach it.
thingsToDo: Theatr Clwyd, one of the leading producing theatres in Wales; the market days; Loggerheads Country Park and the limestone gorge of the Alyn; and the climb onto the ridge at Moel Famau nearby.
whenToVisit: Year-round; the theatre and markets make it a good wet-weather and off-season base.
localTip: Start a ridge walk from Loggerheads Country Park just west of Mold — the wooded limestone gorge of the River Alyn is a lovely warm-up before the climb onto the open heather.

faqs.q: Is Mold easy to reach from England?
faqs.a: Yes — Mold, in Flintshire, is the easternmost town of the Clwydian area and the closest to the motorway network, roughly an hour from Manchester and Liverpool and close to Chester. That makes it a convenient base for a quick scenic escape from the north-west of England.

faqs.q: What is there to do in Mold?
faqs.a: Mold has a lively market, the well-regarded Theatr Clwyd, and easy access to Loggerheads Country Park and the wooded Alyn gorge just to the west, with the Clwydian ridge and Moel Famau a short drive beyond for walking.

name: Corwen
lead: Owain Glyndŵr's town on the upper Dee.
intro: Corwen is a small town on the upper Dee between the Clwydian Range and the Berwyn mountains, strongly associated with Owain Glyndŵr, who raised his standard nearby and is commemorated by a statue in the square. It is a quiet, well-placed base between two ranges of hills.
staying: A good-value, central base for both the Clwydian and Berwyn hills and the Dee valley, with Llangollen a short drive downstream.
thingsToDo: The Owain Glyndŵr statue and heritage; the walks into the Berwyn mountains and up to the Glyndŵr's Seat viewpoint; the restored Corwen station on the Llangollen Railway; and the upper Dee valley.
whenToVisit: Spring to autumn for the hills; a quiet base in any season, and handy for the Llangollen attractions without Llangollen's crowds.
localTip: Walk up to "Glyndŵr's Seat" above the town for a wide view over the Dee valley — the same country the man himself campaigned across six hundred years ago.

faqs.q: What is Corwen's connection to Owain Glyndŵr?
faqs.a: Corwen lies at the heart of Owain Glyndŵr's territory, close to his manor at Glyndyfrdwy where he was proclaimed Prince of Wales in 1400 at the start of his revolt. The town commemorates him with a prominent statue in its square.

faqs.q: Is Corwen a good base for the Berwyn and Clwydian hills?
faqs.a: Yes. Corwen sits on the upper Dee between the Berwyn mountains to the south and the Clwydian Range to the north, giving access to both, plus the Dee valley and nearby Llangollen. It is a quiet, good-value alternative to the busier towns.

name: Denbigh
lead: A hilltop castle over a walled market town.
intro: Denbigh is a historic market town in the Vale of Clwyd, crowned by the substantial ruins of a medieval castle and walled upper town on the hill above. It sits on the western side of the vale, looking across to the Clwydian ridge, with H. M. Stanley — of "Dr Livingstone, I presume" — among its sons.
staying: A quiet, historic base on the far side of the Vale of Clwyd from the ridge, good value and well placed for the whole range and the north coast.
thingsToDo: Denbigh Castle and the town walls; the medieval Burgess Gate; the walks in the Vale of Clwyd; and easy reach of Moel Famau and the ridge across the valley.
whenToVisit: Spring to autumn for the walking and the castle; a calm year-round base.
localTip: Climb to the castle and walk what survives of the walls at dusk — the hilltop ruin catches the last light over the whole Vale of Clwyd and the ridge beyond.

faqs.q: Can you visit Denbigh Castle?
faqs.a: Yes — Denbigh Castle is a substantial 13th-century ruin on the hill above the town, managed by Cadw, with a striking triple-towered gatehouse and surviving stretches of the walled upper town. It gives wide views over the Vale of Clwyd.

faqs.q: Is Denbigh a good base for the Clwydian Range?
faqs.a: Denbigh sits on the western side of the Vale of Clwyd, across the valley from the main Clwydian ridge, so Moel Famau and the hillfort walks are a short drive away. It is a quiet, historic and good-value base for exploring the range and the north coast.

name: Cowbridge
lead: The Vale's market town, with a serious high street.
intro: Cowbridge is the genteel market town at the centre of the Vale of Glamorgan, a broad Georgian-and-medieval high street of independent shops, delis and restaurants that has become one of the most sought-after addresses in south Wales. It sits amid gentle farmland, minutes from the heritage coast.
staying: A comfortable, foodie base for exploring the Vale, close to both Cardiff and the coast, with the best evening options in the area.
thingsToDo: The independent shops and restaurants of the high street; the physic garden and the surviving town wall; and easy drives to the heritage coast at Llantwit Major, Nash Point and Southerndown.
whenToVisit: Year-round — as an inland market town it is far less seasonal than the coast, and a reliable base when the seaside fills up.
localTip: Use Cowbridge as your evening base and the heritage coast as your day out — the beaches and cliffs are fifteen minutes south, but the good food is all in town.

faqs.q: Why is Cowbridge popular?
faqs.a: Cowbridge is known for its attractive Georgian and medieval high street lined with independent shops, delis and restaurants, set in gentle countryside between Cardiff and the Glamorgan Heritage Coast. That mix of good food, character and location has made it one of the most desirable towns in south Wales.

faqs.q: Is Cowbridge a good base for the Glamorgan coast?
faqs.a: Yes. Cowbridge sits inland at the centre of the Vale of Glamorgan, roughly fifteen minutes from the heritage coast beaches at Llantwit Major, Nash Point and Southerndown, while offering the area's best choice of restaurants and shops for the evenings.

name: Llantwit Major
lead: An ancient town of saints, beside the heritage coast.
intro: Llantwit Major claims one of the earliest centres of learning in Britain — a monastic school founded by St Illtud in the fifth century — and keeps a remarkable early-medieval church full of carved Celtic crosses. It sits right on the Glamorgan Heritage Coast, with a dramatic rocky beach below the town.
staying: The pick of the heritage-coast bases, combining real history with a beach and cliff walks on the doorstep, and Cowbridge and Cardiff both close.
thingsToDo: The Church of St Illtud and its Celtic crosses; the medieval town centre; Llantwit Major beach and the striped cliffs of the heritage coast; and the coast path to Nash Point and St Donats.
whenToVisit: Late spring to early autumn for the beach and cliffs; the town and church are a year-round draw.
localTip: Walk the coast path west from the beach towards Nash Point at low tide — the striped Jurassic rock platforms and the working lighthouse are the best of the whole heritage coast.

faqs.q: Why is Llantwit Major historically important?
faqs.a: Llantwit Major is the site of a monastic school founded by St Illtud around the fifth century, often described as one of the earliest centres of learning in Britain. Its Church of St Illtud holds an outstanding collection of early-medieval Celtic carved stones and crosses.

faqs.q: What is the Glamorgan Heritage Coast?
faqs.a: The Glamorgan Heritage Coast is a protected stretch of striped Jurassic limestone cliffs and rocky beaches running west from Barry, taking in Llantwit Major, Nash Point and Southerndown. It offers dramatic clifftop walking within easy reach of Cardiff.

name: Penarth
lead: A Victorian pier and promenade, minutes from Cardiff.
intro: Penarth is an elegant Victorian seaside town on the eastern edge of the Vale, effectively Cardiff-by-the-sea, with a restored pier, a curving esplanade and clifftop gardens. It combines a genteel resort feel with immediate access to the capital just across the barrage.
staying: The base for those who want a seaside town with a city day built in — Cardiff Bay is a walk or short hop across the barrage, and the heritage coast is a short drive west.
thingsToDo: The pier and pavilion and the esplanade; the walk over the Cardiff Bay Barrage into the city; the clifftop path to Lavernock; and Cosmeston Lakes and medieval village just south.
whenToVisit: Year-round as a town; summer for the pier and seafront. Very easy to reach from Cardiff.
localTip: Walk across the Cardiff Bay Barrage from Penarth into the Bay — a flat, breezy stroll that links a Victorian pier to the modern waterfront in twenty minutes on foot.

faqs.q: Is Penarth close to Cardiff?
faqs.a: Yes — Penarth sits directly across Cardiff Bay from the city, linked by the Cardiff Bay Barrage, which you can walk or cycle across in around twenty minutes. It makes an ideal base for combining a seaside stay with easy days in the Welsh capital.

faqs.q: What is there to do in Penarth?
faqs.a: Penarth offers a restored Victorian pier and pavilion, a seafront esplanade and clifftop gardens, coastal walks towards Lavernock, and the nearby Cosmeston Lakes and reconstructed medieval village — all within easy reach of Cardiff Bay.

name: Barry
lead: Barry Island, a pleasure beach and a sitcom afterlife.
intro: Barry is the largest town in the Vale, and its seaside quarter, Barry Island, is a classic Welsh pleasure beach — a wide arc of sand, a funfair and a promenade — given a second life as the setting for the sitcom Gavin & Stacey. Behind the resort front it is a busy working town with a long dockland history.
staying: A lively, family-friendly and good-value base at the eastern end of the heritage coast, with the beach and funfair on hand and Cardiff and Cowbridge close.
thingsToDo: Whitmore Bay and the Barry Island promenade and funfair; the Gavin & Stacey filming locations; Porthkerry Country Park and its viaduct; and the pebble beach at the Knap.
whenToVisit: Summer for the beach and funfair; the resort is quieter but still open around the shoulder seasons.
localTip: Walk west from the resort to Porthkerry Country Park — woods and cliffs under a huge railway viaduct, with a pebble beach at the bottom, a world away from the funfair a mile back.

faqs.q: Is Barry Island worth visiting?
faqs.a: Barry Island is a traditional seaside resort with a wide sandy beach (Whitmore Bay), a promenade and a funfair, and it draws visitors as the filming location for the sitcom Gavin & Stacey. It is an easy, family-friendly day out close to Cardiff.

faqs.q: What is Porthkerry Country Park?
faqs.a: Porthkerry Country Park, on the edge of Barry, is a wooded valley leading to a pebble beach beneath a tall Victorian railway viaduct. It offers walking, picnicking and a quieter alternative to the Barry Island resort front nearby.

name: Southerndown
lead: Dunraven Bay and the cliffs that stand in for everywhere.
intro: Southerndown is a small village on the Glamorgan Heritage Coast beside Dunraven Bay, a dramatic beach of sand and rock beneath striped limestone cliffs and the terraced remains of a lost clifftop mansion. The scenery is so cinematic it regularly stands in for other coasts on screen, including in Doctor Who.
staying: A scenic, low-key base right on the heritage coast, quieter than the resort towns and superb for cliff walks, with Cowbridge and Bridgend close for supplies.
thingsToDo: Dunraven Bay and the walled gardens of the vanished Dunraven Castle; the clifftop walks east towards Ogmore and west towards Nash Point; and rock-pooling and fossils on the beach at low tide.
whenToVisit: Spring to autumn for the beach and cliffs; the coast is dramatic in any season and often filmed in winter.
localTip: Explore the terraced walled garden of the demolished Dunraven Castle above the bay — a strange, atmospheric survival, and the viewpoint gives you the whole striped sweep of the heritage coast.

faqs.q: What is Dunraven Bay at Southerndown?
faqs.a: Dunraven Bay is the beach at Southerndown on the Glamorgan Heritage Coast, backed by dramatic striped limestone cliffs and the walled gardens of the demolished Dunraven Castle. Its striking scenery has featured in productions including Doctor Who.

faqs.q: Is Southerndown good for walking?
faqs.a: Yes — Southerndown sits on the Wales Coast Path, with cliff walks in both directions along the Glamorgan Heritage Coast, towards Ogmore-by-Sea and the Nash Point lighthouse. The beach is also known for rock pools and fossils at low tide.
